check:0:1.a:
"Both go up" gets one part right. Precision usually does go up. The part it misses is recall.

Quick definitions first:
- **Precision**: of everything the model said "yes" to, how many were really yes?
- **Recall**: of all the real yes cases, how many did the model catch?

Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 means fewer scores clear the bar. So the model says "yes" less often.

That usually helps precision. The yeses that remain are the confident ones, so fewer of them are wrong.

Recall is different. It can never go up when you raise the threshold. Every real yes case you caught at 0.9 was already caught at 0.5. Raising the bar can only keep those catches or lose some. Any real yes with a score between 0.5 and 0.9 now gets missed. So recall stays the same or drops, and it usually drops.

That is the trade-off the lesson mentions. One side improves while the other pays for it.

"Precision goes up, recall goes down" is better because it names that trade-off: fewer yeses make each yes more trustworthy, but more real cases slip through.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Recall goes up, precision goes down”?
check:0:2.a:
The option "Recall goes up, precision goes down" gets one thing right. Precision and recall usually move in opposite directions when you change the threshold. But it has the directions backwards.

Two quick definitions:
- **Precision**: of everything the model called "yes," how many really were yes.
- **Recall**: of all the real yes cases, how many the model caught.

Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 makes the model stricter. Fewer scores clear the bar, so it says "yes" less often.

- Fewer "yes" calls means more real yes cases slip through. So **recall goes down**.
- The "yes" calls that remain are the ones the model was most confident about. Those are more likely to be right. So **precision usually goes up**.

Using the lesson's scores `[0.9, 0.65, 0.4]`: at 0.5 you get two yeses. At 0.9 you get just one, the most confident.

"Precision goes up, recall goes down" is better because it matches what a stricter threshold does: fewer, more confident "yes" calls.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Lower, so more payments get flagged”?
check:1:0.a:
Lowering the threshold does have one upside. More payments get flagged, so you catch more real fraud. That is called higher **recall**: of all the real fraud, how much you catch.

But it misses the actual problem. The checkers are drowning in **false alarms**. A false alarm is a payment flagged as fraud that turns out to be fine. A lower threshold means more scores land at or above it. So more payments get flagged, and many of those extra ones are innocent. The pile of false alarms grows. You would make the checkers' day worse.

What they need is higher **precision**: of the payments you flag, how many are really fraud. Precision usually goes up when you flag fewer, more confident cases.

Using the lesson's scores `[0.9, 0.65, 0.4]`:

```python
# t = 0.5 -> [1, 1, 0]   two flagged
# t = 0.3 -> [1, 1, 1]   all three flagged, more work for checkers
```

Moving the threshold higher is better because it flags only the most confident cases. That cuts false alarms, at the cost of missing some fraud.

judge.notes: No substantive problems. The closing explanation runs to two sentences where one was asked for, which is minor.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nowhere: thresholds don't change alarms”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why not "Nowhere: thresholds don't change alarms"?**

This option gets one thing right. Moving the threshold does not change the model. The scores stay exactly the same. You are not retraining anything.

But it misses the main point of this lesson. An alarm is not the score itself. An alarm is a payment whose score is at or above the threshold. So the threshold directly decides which payments get flagged.

Take the lesson's scores again:

```python
scores = [0.9, 0.65, 0.4]
# t = 0.5  -> [1, 1, 0]   two payments flagged
# t = 0.7  -> [1, 0, 0]   one payment flagged
```

Same scores, but a different number of alarms. A **false alarm** (also called a false positive) is a flagged payment that was actually fine. When fewer payments get flagged, there are usually fewer false alarms. That is the "higher precision" trade the lesson describes. **Precision** means the share of flags that were real fraud.

**Why "Higher, so fewer payments get flagged" is better:** raising the threshold means only higher-scoring payments get flagged, so the checkers see fewer false alarms. The cost is that some real fraud may slip through, which means lower **recall** (the share of real fraud you catch).

judge.notes: No significant problems; the explanation matches the lesson, stays under 200 words, and gives no exercise solution (the closing 'why better' part runs to two sentences instead of one, which is a minor style issue).

check:2:0.q: Why not “Try more thresholds on it”?
check:2:0.a:
"Try more thresholds on it" gets one thing right. Searching for a better threshold is a good instinct. But that search belongs on the validation set, and you've already done it there.

The test set has a different job. It stands in for new data the model has never seen. Its score is meant to answer one question: "How well will this work in real life?"

If you try thresholds on the test set and keep the best one, you are tuning on it. The threshold starts to fit quirks of those particular examples, partly by luck. The test score then looks better than real-world performance will be. This is called **overfitting to the test set**: doing well on the data you tuned on, but not on fresh data. You also have nothing untouched left to check against, so you can't spot the problem.

In MLflow terms, the test metric you log would no longer be an honest number. It would be one more tuning result.

"Check 0.7 on it once" is better because a single, untuned check keeps the test score an honest preview of how 0.7 will do on new data.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Skip it, validation was enough”?
check:2:1.a:
"Skip it, validation was enough" gets one thing right. Validation did its job. It helped you choose 0.7, and you should not keep tuning on any other data.

What it misses is that the validation score is now a bit too hopeful. You tried many thresholds on that same data and kept the winner. Some of that win may come from quirks of those exact examples, not from the threshold being truly good. This is called **overfitting**: fitting the data you tuned on so closely that results look better than they will on new data.

The **test set** is data you set aside and never looked at while choosing. It acts like fresh, real-world examples. Running 0.7 on it once gives you an honest estimate of how the model will do after launch. If the test result is much worse than validation, that is a warning you would miss by skipping it.

"Once" matters too. If you kept adjusting the threshold after seeing test results, the test set would become just another validation set.

"Check 0.7 on it once" is better because it gives an honest, unbiased score on data that played no part in picking the threshold.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Don't compare decimals with ==” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Computers store decimals in binary (only 0s and 1s). Many simple decimals, like 0.1, can't be stored exactly, so each one is saved as a very close approximation. Usually you never notice. But `==` asks "are these exactly equal?", and tiny leftovers make the answer "no" when you expect "yes".

```python
print(0.1 + 0.2)          # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # False
print(1 - 0.9 >= 0.1)     # False, because 1 - 0.9 is 0.09999999999999998
```

Here is why that matters in real work. Say a score comes out of some arithmetic and should land exactly on your threshold of 0.1. The rule is "at or above means yes". But the stored score is a hair below 0.1, so it quietly becomes a 0. Nothing crashes. Your counts are just slightly off. A threshold you logged in MLflow might then behave differently when someone reruns it.

The same trap hits similarity scores (numbers saying how alike two things are). Checking `score == 1.0` to find "identical" items can miss true matches.

The fix is to compare with a small allowed gap. In Python, `math.isclose(a, b)` asks "are these close enough to count as equal?"

judge.notes: The MLflow rerun sentence is vague and a bit misleading, since the same code would give the same result on a rerun. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit. Neither is a clear failure.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The test score looks great, then drops in real use.** This often means the threshold was tuned on the test set. The test set should be checked once, after tuning on the validation set (the practice data you tune on).
- **Accuracy is high, but the business is unhappy.** Too many real cases slip through, which is low **recall**. Or too many false alarms show up, which is low **precision**. The threshold that is best for accuracy may not be the one the business needs.
- **The number of "yes" answers shifts sharply between runs** without a clear reason. The threshold may have changed quietly.
- **You can't tell which threshold produced a result.** It was never saved as a parameter in MLflow.

**Quickest check**

Open your MLflow runs. Confirm each run logged a `threshold` parameter. Then compare its validation numbers with the single test result. A big gap between them is a red flag. A test result that was used to pick the threshold is also a red flag. Finally, check precision and recall at that threshold. Make sure they match what the business actually cares about.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where picking a threshold needs extra care.

**1. Data that changes over time.** The threshold is tuned on past data, but scores can shift as users or spammers change their habits. Re-check precision and recall on fresh labeled examples on a regular schedule. Log each new threshold as an MLflow parameter so you can compare old and new runs.

**2. Very little data.** With only a few validation examples, the "best" threshold may just be luck, because one example can flip the winner. Use cross-validation, which means splitting the data several different ways and averaging the results, before trusting a threshold.

**3. An LLM or RAG app.** An LLM (a large language model, like the one behind a chatbot) usually returns text, not a score, so there may be nothing to put a threshold on. In a RAG app (one that looks up documents before answering), you can use the retrieval similarity score instead, which says how close a document is to the question. Tune that cutoff on a labeled validation set, just like in this lesson.

learn:term.a:
A **threshold** is the cut-off line you pick to turn a score into a yes or no.

Think of the height sign at a theme park ride. Kids at or above the line get on. Kids below it don't. The ride doesn't change. Only where you draw the line changes.

A classifier works the same way. It doesn't say "spam" or "not spam." It gives a **score**, like `0.65`, meaning roughly "how spam-like this looks." You decide the line. At or above it means yes (`1`). Below it means no (`0`).

In the lesson's example, the scores are `[0.9, 0.65, 0.4]`:

- With a threshold of `0.5`, both `0.9` and `0.65` clear the line. You get `[1, 1, 0]`.
- With a threshold of `0.7`, only `0.9` clears it. You get `[1, 0, 0]`.

Same model, same scores. The middle item flipped just because the line moved.

A higher line means fewer yes answers. Those yeses are more often correct (higher **precision**), but you miss more real ones (lower **recall**).

That's why the MLflow snippet logs `threshold` as a parameter. It's a choice you make and record, like any other setting.

check:0:1.q: Why not “It forgets because it is broken”?
check:0:1.a:
"It forgets because it is broken" gets one thing right. The symptom is real: today the assistant does not recall yesterday's chat.

But it gets the cause wrong. Nothing is broken. This is how an LLM normally works.

Each time your code sends a request to the model, that is one **call**. The model reads only what is in that call: your instructions, the question, and anything else you include. When the call ends, it keeps nothing. It has no memory of its own between calls.

So yesterday's conversation is not lost because of a fault. It simply was not sent today. If you resend the earlier messages, the model can see them again and pick up where it left off.

Calling it "broken" also points you the wrong way. You might hunt for a bug or a repair. The real fix is a design choice: decide what to send with each call, and keep it within the **context window**, the limit on how many tokens the model can read at once.

"It only sees what is sent in each call" is better because it names the real cause and shows the fix: resend what the model needs.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Its tokens ran out overnight”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a reasonable guess. Tokens do matter here. The **context window** (how many tokens the model can take in at once) is counted in tokens. If you send a very long conversation, the oldest parts can fall outside that limit.

But that isn't what happened. Tokens aren't a supply that drains overnight. The model doesn't keep yesterday's chat stored somewhere, slowly running low. It keeps nothing between calls at all.

Each call starts fresh. The model only reads what you send in that call: your instructions, the question, and any earlier messages you choose to resend. Yesterday it answered well because yesterday's messages were in the prompt. Today they weren't resent, so to the model they don't exist.

So the problem isn't running out. It's that the conversation was never sent. If your app resends the earlier messages, the model "remembers" them again.

"It only sees what is sent in each call" is the better answer. It names the real cause: the model has no memory between calls, so anything not resent is invisible to it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the signs that something about tokens or the context window has slipped.

**Errors or cut-off answers.** The call fails with a "too many tokens" error. Or the answer stops mid-sentence. That often means you forgot to leave room for the answer, not just the prompt.

**The model "forgets."** It ignores yesterday's chat or your new policy. Usually that text was never sent in this call. Remember, it only sees what you send each time.

**Costs creep up.** Your bill grows faster than your number of users. Every call is resending a big document, and you pay for those tokens every time.

**Quality drops as prompts grow.** Testing with short prompts looks great. Then real use, with long chats and many documents, gives vaguer or wrong answers even though the fact was in there. That is context rot.

**Quickest check:** log the token count of each part of one real prompt: instructions, question, resent messages, documents. Add the room kept for the answer. Compare the total with the model's window. If one part dwarfs the rest, start trimming there.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where "add it up and compare with the window" needs extra care.

**1. Your token counts are guesses.**
The "750 words is about 1,000 tokens" rule holds roughly for English prose. Code, numbers, and other languages often split into many more tokens, and each model splits text its own way. Count with the tokenizer (the tool that splits text into tokens) for the exact model you call, and leave some spare room.

**2. A chat that keeps growing.**
Each turn resends earlier messages, so a prompt that fit on turn one can overflow by turn twenty. Check the total before every call, not once. When it gets close, drop or summarize the oldest messages.

**3. "It fits" is not the same as "it works well."**
Because of context rot, answers can get worse long before you hit the limit, and you pay for every token on every call. Aim well below the window. Send only the few passages that answer this question.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that code, numbers and other languages split into more tokens goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and 'context rot' is named without a short explanation.

learn:term.a:
The **context window** is how much text the model can take in at once. It is counted in tokens, the small pieces of words the model reads.

Think of a whiteboard in a meeting room. The model can only work with what is on the board right now. If something isn't written there, the model never sees it. After each call, the board is wiped clean. Want it to know yesterday's chat? Write it up again.

The board also has a fixed size. Anything past its edge isn't seen.

In the lesson's example, three things go on the board for one question:
- the instructions, about 50 tokens
- the policy page, about 6,000 tokens
- the question, about 15 tokens

That's a little over 6,000 tokens. The lesson doesn't give the window's size, so we can't say how much room is left. We do know that all of it is read, and paid for, on every question.

A bigger board doesn't mean you should fill it. Longer prompts tend to give less reliable answers. Send only what this question needs.

check:0:1.q: Why not “An LLM that writes about each invoice”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair thought. An LLM can read an invoice's details and write something sensible, like "this customer has paid late before, so watch it." That part is real. LLMs are good at reading and writing language.

But this job isn't about language. It's a prediction: late or on time. And you already have the perfect material for that. Three years of invoices, each with the right answer attached. Those answers are called **labels**.

An LLM never learned from your labelled invoices. Its provider trained it on general text, so it would be guessing from general knowledge, not from your own history.

It also gives you text, not a number. You'd have to read and check every note. A trained model gives a score, like "80% likely to be late." You can set a **threshold** on that score, a cut-off like "flag anything over 70%." You can also test it against past invoices to see how often it's right.

And an LLM costs more for each invoice it handles.

A model trained on past invoices is better because it learns directly from your labelled examples and gives a score you can test and act on.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A fixed rule on the invoice amount”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a fair guess. The lesson says to try the simplest tool first, and a rule is the simplest. So checking for a rule is the right instinct.

**What it gets right:** Invoice amount might matter. Big invoices could be paid late more often. A rule like "flag invoices over $5,000" is cheap, fast, and easy to explain.

**What it misses:** A rule only works when it *always* gives the right answer. Lateness doesn't work like that. It probably depends on many details together: which customer it is, their past payment habits, the payment terms (how many days they have to pay), the time of year. A small invoice from a slow payer may be late. A big one from a reliable customer may not. One fixed cut-off on amount can't capture that mix. Nobody knows the exact rule in advance anyway.

**The clue in the question:** you have three years of invoices already marked "late" or "on time". Those marks are **labels**, the right answers a model can learn from.

A model trained on past invoices is better because it finds the patterns across all those details for you, then gives each new invoice a likelihood score.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the wrong kind of AI was picked**

- **An LLM doing a rule's job.** The same refund question gets different answers on different runs. Costs and wait times are high for something a single `if` line could decide.
- **A plain LLM where answers must come from your documents.** Replies sound confident but quote policies you don't have. This is called a "hallucination": the model makes something up that sounds right.
- **A trained model with no real labels.** Labels are past cases with the known right answer. Without enough of them, the test score looks great, then drops once real invoices arrive. Or there is simply nothing honest to test on.
- **An LLM where a trained model fits.** You get text back but no score. So you can't set a threshold, meaning a cut-off like "flag anything over 70% likely late."
- **An agent where no actions are needed.** Traces, the step-by-step logs of what the agent did, show long chains of tool calls just to answer a question.

**Quickest check**

Take 10 to 20 real past cases where you know the right answer. Try the simplest tool on them first. If it gets them right, stop there. Only step up when it clearly fails.

judge.notes: No real problems. It runs to about 200 words, and the hallucination term and the '10 to 20 cases' figure come from outside the lesson, but neither contradicts it.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The rule keeps changing.** A rule works only while the answer stays fixed. If exceptions keep piling up, look at whether a trained model fits better, since it can learn the pattern from labelled past cases.

**2. The data shifts over time.** A model trained on last year's invoices may score badly once customers start paying differently. This slow change is called **drift**, so retrain on recent cases and keep comparing its scores with what really happened.

**3. One job holds several kinds of work.** A bigger system, like an email helper, might read text, check a policy, predict lateness and update an order. Don't give the whole thing to an agent. Split it into parts, then pick the simplest tool for each part.

learn:term.a:
They are two different kinds of thing. One is a method. The other is the data that method needs.

**Machine learning** is the method. It means building a model, a program that learns patterns from past cases instead of following rules you wrote by hand.

**Labels** are the right answers attached to those past cases. They are what the model learns from.

So machine learning is the learning. Labels are the answer key it learns against.

**An everyday comparison:** think of studying with flashcards. The answer on the back of each card is the label. You, getting better by checking yourself against those answers, are the machine learning.

**The lesson's example:**

- **Past cases:** three years of invoices.
- **Labels:** the mark on each invoice, "paid late" or "on time".
- **Machine learning:** the model finds patterns that link an invoice's details to its label. Then it scores a new invoice on how likely it is to be late.

**How they work together:** without labels, the model has nothing to learn from and nothing to test against. That is why labelled examples are one of the gates for a good use case.

check:0:1.q: Why not “A bigger GPU with more memory”?
check:0:1.a:
A bigger GPU solves a different problem. GPU memory matters once the model's files are on your computer. Then the question is whether the weights, and for training everything else, fit. The lesson spends a lot of time on that, so it's a fair thing to think of.

But here the notebook can't even download the files. Nothing has reached the GPU yet. The page tells you why: the model is **gated**. Anyone can see the page, but the makers only hand over the files to people who have logged in and accepted their licence. No amount of memory changes who Hugging Face lets download.

This is just what happened with `embeddinggemma` in the lab. The lab's computer had no token, so the training files couldn't be fetched. That was a fact about access, not about the hardware or the model.

"To accept it and use an access token" is better because it fixes the real blocker. You accept the licence in your browser. Then you give your code a read-only token, a secret key like a password, so Hugging Face knows the download is allowed.

check:0:2.q: Why not “To load it in 16-bit instead”?
check:0:2.a:
"Load it in 16-bit instead" mixes up two different problems.

What it gets right: 16-bit (half precision) is a real choice. Each weight takes 2 bytes instead of 4, so the model needs about half the memory. That helps when a model is too big for your GPU's memory.

What it misses: here the problem is not memory. Your notebook can't download the files at all. The model is **gated**: anyone can see its page, but only people who accept the makers' licence can fetch the files. The number of bits each weight uses changes nothing about that. You can't load any version, 16-bit or 32-bit, of files you don't have.

This is the same wall the lab hit with `embeddinggemma`. There was no token on the computer, so the files for training couldn't be fetched. It was a fact about access, not about the model's size.

"To accept it and use an access token" is better because it fixes the real problem. You accept the licence in your browser, then give your code a read-only token (a secret key that proves who you are to programs), and the download is allowed.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it never defines GPU, and it leaves out the log-in step, but neither makes it wrong.

check:1:1.a:
"About 2 GB" counts only the model file. That part is right: training does need the weights in memory, and in 32-bit they take the full 2 GB. But that is only what *running* the model needs.

Training holds more beside every weight:

- **A gradient** for each weight. That is the number saying which way the weight should move. It is the same size as the weights, so another 2 GB.
- **The optimiser's two running averages** for each weight. The optimiser is the rule that turns a gradient into an actual change. AdamW, the common one, keeps two averages per weight, so 4 GB more.

That makes four numbers for every weight, not one. 2 GB + 2 GB + 4 GB = 8 GB. The in-between numbers (activations) come on top of that.

Think of booking a room for a talk. "About 2 GB" counts only the speaker and forgets everyone else who comes.

"About 8 GB" is better because it counts all four numbers training keeps for each weight: the weight, its gradient, and AdamW's two averages.

check:1:2.a:
"About 4 GB" gets part of it right. It counts the weights (the 2 GB file) and a gradient for every weight. A gradient is the note saying which way each weight should move. That's another 2 GB, so 4 GB so far.

What it misses is the optimiser. The optimiser is the rule that turns each gradient into an actual move. The common one, AdamW, keeps two running averages for every weight. These are like two notebooks tracking how that weight has been moving lately. Each one is the same size as the file, so that's 4 GB more.

So for every weight, training keeps four numbers side by side:

- the weight itself: 2 GB
- its gradient: 2 GB
- AdamW's first running average: 2 GB
- AdamW's second running average: 2 GB

The in-between numbers (activations) come on top of that. The question set those aside.

"About 8 GB" is better because it counts all four numbers per weight, which is four times the file, not just two.

check:2:1.q: Why not “It left out half of the weights”?
check:2:1.a:
It's a fair guess. The file really is about half the size, so something was halved. But it wasn't the number of weights.

**What it misses:** a model is its weights. Each weight does a job, so you can't drop half and keep the same model. A model missing half its weights would give very different, mostly broken answers. In the lab, Ollama's copy of bge-large gave the **same answers** as the Hugging Face copy. That only makes sense if every weight is still there.

**What actually shrank:** the space each weight takes. bge-large has 335 million weights either way.

- In 32-bit (full precision), each weight takes 4 bytes. That gives the 1.3 GB file.
- In 16-bit (half precision), each weight takes 2 bytes. That gives about 0.67 GB.

Same count of weights, half the bytes each. Each number is kept a little less exactly, but not enough to change the answers here.

"It keeps each weight in 16 bits" is better because it explains the halved size and the unchanged answers: all the weights are kept, each in half the space.

check:2:2.q: Why not “It is a different, smaller model”?
check:2:2.a:
It is a fair guess. A model with fewer weights really would make a smaller file. So the idea that "fewer bytes means something changed" is right.

What it misses is *what* changed. The number of weights stayed the same. The size of each one changed.

Look at the numbers in the lesson. `bge-large` has 335 million weights. In 32-bit (full precision), each weight takes 4 bytes, which gives the 1.3 GB file in your cache. In 16-bit (half precision), each weight takes 2 bytes. Same count, half the bytes each, so the file is about half the size. The "about half" matches this exactly.

There is a second clue. In the lab, Ollama's copy and the Hugging Face copy gave the same answers. A different, smaller model would usually give different answers. Storing each number a little less exactly barely changes the results.

So it was one model, written down two ways.

"It keeps each weight in 16 bits" is better because it explains why the file is exactly about half the size while the model and its answers stay the same.

judge.notes: No real failure; the only blemishes are the loose wording 'matches this exactly' and 'exactly about half' for what the lesson calls 'about half', and the claim that a smaller model 'would usually give different answers', which goes slightly beyond the lesson.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the memory sum was skipped**

- Training stops with an **out-of-memory** error. That means the GPU's memory ran out. It often comes in the first few steps, or right after you raise the batch size. The batch size is how many examples go in each step.
- Training runs for a while, then crashes partway through. Another job may have loaded a model into Ollama and taken memory you counted on.
- The whole computer slows down or freezes. On shared memory, the GPU is squeezing every other program.
- Your plan only counted the model file, say 1.3 GB, and felt roomy. Training needs far more.

**Signs access was the problem**

- Fetching the files fails with "gated", "unauthorised" or "401". That points to a missing token or an unaccepted licence. It says nothing about the model itself.

**The quickest check**

Before you train, redo the sum by hand. Take the weights' size four times over. Add the in-between numbers. Compare the total with the memory that is free right now, not the total on the label. Then watch memory use during the first few steps.

judge.notes: Passes. The quickest check restates the lesson's own idea in prose (four times the weights, plus the in-between numbers, compared with free memory), which is close to the exercise logic but is not code or the answer to a Check question.

learn:stops.a:
The rule is a good first estimate. Here is where it needs extra care.

**Training in 16-bit.** Halving the bytes per number does not halve everything. Many setups still keep the optimiser's running averages, plus a spare copy of the weights, in 32-bit. Count the bytes for each part on its own instead of assuming one size for all.

**Training only a small add-on.** With LoRA (a method that freezes the big model and trains a few small extra weights), only those extras get gradients and running averages. The big model's weights are held just once, so the real total can be far below your estimate.

**Free memory that moves.** On a shared GPU, the free amount can drop in the middle of a run, for example when another job loads a model into Ollama. Check against the worst case, not today's number. Then keep some memory spare, or turn on gradient checkpointing.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 16-bit and LoRA points go beyond the lesson but are accurate and do not contradict it.

learn:term.a:
**Hugging Face** is a website. Model makers publish their model files there. These files are the model's **weights**: big files of numbers that make up the model. Hugging Face lives on the internet, and anyone can browse it.

The **cache** is your own copy of those files. It is saved on your computer the first time your code downloads them. After that, your code reads the local copy instead of downloading again.

Think of a shop and your pantry. You buy groceries at the shop once, then cook from the pantry every night. You only go back to the shop for something new.

They work together. Your code asks for a model by name. If the files are already in the cache, it loads them straight from your disk. If not, it fetches them from Hugging Face and keeps them in the cache for next time.

In the lab, the embedding model `bge-large` was downloaded from Hugging Face once. An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers for search. Its 1.3 GB of weights then sat in the cache, and the lab ran it from there.

judge.notes: No real problems. The check-by-name and fetch-if-missing behaviour goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:1.a:
"Precision 0.2, recall 0.8" uses the right two numbers but puts them in the wrong places. The numbers are swapped.

**Precision** asks: of the emails the filter flagged, how many were really spam? The filter flagged 10 emails, and 8 of those were spam. So 8 out of 10 were right, which is 0.8. Here the bottom of the fraction (the denominator) is the 10 flagged emails.

**Recall** asks: of all the spam that existed, how much did the filter catch? There were 40 spam emails, and it caught 8. So 8 out of 40 were caught, which is 0.2. Here the denominator is the 40 spam emails in total.

The swapped answer describes a different filter. That filter would catch most of the spam but flag lots of good email too. Ours is the reverse. It is careful, since its flags are usually right, but it misses most of the spam.

A handy check: precision divides by what the model *flagged*, and recall divides by what it *should have* flagged.

"Precision 0.8, recall 0.2" is better because it matches each question to the right denominator: 10 flagged emails for precision, 40 real spam emails for recall.

check:0:2.a:
"Precision 0.8, recall 0.8" gets half of it right.

**What it gets right:** precision really is 0.8. Precision asks: of the emails the filter flagged, how many were truly spam? It flagged 10, and 8 were spam. That's 8 out of 10, so 0.8.

**What it misses:** recall asks a different question. Of all the spam that existed, how much did the filter catch? There were 40 spam emails, and it caught only 8. The other 32 slipped into the inbox. Catching 8 out of 40 is one in five, which is 0.2.

The 0.8 answer quietly reuses the flagged pile of 10 for both numbers. Recall has to look at the whole pile of real spam, including the ones the filter never flagged. Those missed ones are called false negatives: the model said "no", but the truth was "yes".

This is the lesson's big point. A filter can look sharp on what it flags while missing most of what matters.

**Why "Precision 0.8, recall 0.2" is better:** it shows that the filter is usually right when it flags something, but it catches only a small share of the spam.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, 99% is an excellent score”?
check:1:0.a:
The 99% figure is real. The model is right on 99 out of every 100 machines. That part of "Yes, 99% is an excellent score" holds up.

The problem is how it gets there. It never thinks about the machines at all. It just says "no breakdown" every time. Since breakdowns are rare, saying "no" is almost always right by luck.

Now look at the one machine that matters: the one that breaks. The model misses it. It would miss every breakdown, forever. That is the whole job, and it fails at it completely.

This is why accuracy (the share of all answers that are right) lies when one kind of case is rare. The easy, common cases swamp the score.

Recall asks: of the breakdowns that really happened, how many did the model catch? Here the answer is none, so recall is zero.

"No, it never catches a breakdown" is better because it judges the model on the rare case you actually care about, not on the easy ones.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Yes, if the test set was large”?
check:1:2.a:
"Yes, if the test set was large" gets one thing right. A bigger test set (the batch of examples you check the model on) makes the 99% figure more trustworthy. With only 10 machines, 99% could be luck. With 10,000, it is a solid number.

But it misses the real problem. A larger test set only makes you more sure the model scores 99%. It does not change what the model does. This model says "no breakdown" every single time. So it scores 99% just because breakdowns are rare. It never flags a single one.

That is why we look at **recall**: of all the machines that really broke down, how many did the model catch? Here the answer is none. Recall is 0. No amount of test data fixes that, because the model never says "yes."

Accuracy (the share of all answers that are right) hides this. The 99 easy "no" cases drown out the 1 case you actually care about.

"No, it never catches a breakdown" is better because it names the real failure: the model misses every breakdown, which is the whole reason it exists.

judge.notes: Minor nit: "with only 10 machines, 99% could be luck" is awkward, since 10 machines can't score 99%, but nothing contradicts the lesson.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Precision: how many it hid were toxic”?
check:2:1.a:
"Precision: how many it hid were toxic" describes precision correctly. It just measures the wrong thing for this goal.

Precision looks only at the comments the filter hid. It asks: of those, how many were really toxic? A high score means the filter rarely hides harmless comments by mistake. Those mistakes are called false positives, or `fp`.

But the question says hiding some harmless comments is fine. The real worry is toxic comments slipping through. Those are false negatives, or `fn`: the filter said "fine" when the comment was toxic. Precision never counts them. They are not in its formula at all.

Here is how that can go wrong. Say there are 100 toxic comments. The filter hides just one, and that one is toxic. Precision is 1 out of 1, which is 100%. That looks perfect. Yet 99 toxic comments got through.

Recall is better because it asks "of all the toxic comments, how many did we catch?", so it directly measures the misses this filter must avoid.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Accuracy: how many it got right overall”?
check:2:2.a:
Accuracy sounds sensible. It counts how many answers were right out of all answers. That part is true, and it's a fine number when the classes are roughly balanced.

The trouble is that toxic comments are rare. Say 1 in 100 comments is toxic. A filter that never hides anything is right 99 times out of 100. That's 99% accuracy, and it catches zero toxic comments. Accuracy is mostly measuring the easy, common case (harmless comments) and hiding the failure you care about.

The goal in this question is to catch nearly every toxic comment, even if some harmless ones get hidden too. Hiding a harmless comment is a "false positive" (flagged, but really fine). Missing a toxic one is a "false negative" (not flagged, but really toxic). Here, false negatives are the costly mistake. Accuracy mixes both mistakes into one number, so it can't tell you how many toxic comments slipped through.

**Recall is better because it measures exactly that: out of all the toxic comments that really exist, how many the filter caught.**

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Return the answer, don't print it” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Printing and returning look alike when you run code by hand. Both seem to "give you the answer." But they do very different jobs.

`print` shows a value on the screen for a human to read. Then the value is gone. `return` hands the value back to whoever called your function, so other code can use it.

The tests are "other code." They call your function and check what comes back. If you only print, the function gives back `None`, which is Python's word for "nothing." The test sees `None` and fails, even though the right number flashed on screen.

The same thing happens in real work. Here is a small example, unrelated to the exercise:

```python
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)

result = double(5)   # screen shows 10
print(result)        # None
```

Now picture passing that into `mlflow.log_metrics({"score": result})`. MLflow would get `None` instead of a number. The run would fail, or your dashboard would be missing the score. Nobody reads the console output later. Only returned values flow into the next step.

So use `print` while debugging. Use `return` for the answer.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Accuracy looks great, but the rare cases slip through.** A 99% score on fraud data sounds impressive. Then real fraud keeps getting through once the model is live.
- **The model almost never says "yes".** If it flags nothing, or close to nothing, it may have learned to always answer "no". That scores high accuracy for free.
- **Recall near 0.** It catches almost none of the cases you care about.
- **Precision near 0, or flags everywhere.** It shouts "yes" so often that people start ignoring the alerts.
- **Only accuracy shows up in your MLflow runs.** If `precision` and `recall` are missing from the logged metrics, nobody checked the rare class.
- **A 0 where you expected a number.** This can mean the model made no "yes" predictions at all. Precision then has nothing to divide by.

**Quickest check**

Count the three piles: `tp`, `fp` and `fn`. Also compare two simple counts: how many real "yes" cases exist, and how many "yes" answers the model gave. If the model's count is tiny or zero, accuracy was hiding the problem.

judge.notes: Minor: tp, fp and fn are used without being spelled out, but the lesson defines them and nothing contradicts the lesson.

learn:stops.a:
**1. An LLM or RAG app instead of a trained model.** Free-text answers have no ready-made yes or no, so first label each answer right or wrong, using a person or a second model acting as a grader. For RAG (retrieval-augmented generation, where the app fetches documents before answering), you can apply the same idea to the fetched documents: precision is how many fetched documents were useful, and recall is how many useful documents it found.

**2. Very few rare cases.** With only 5 fraud cases, one miss drops recall by 20 points, so the numbers jump around. Gather more labelled examples, and report the raw counts next to the percentages.

**3. Data that changes over time.** Fraud tricks change, so last month's precision and recall can quietly go stale. Re-measure on fresh labelled data regularly, and log each run with `mlflow.log_metrics` so you can spot a drop.

learn:term.a:
Picture a metal detector at the beach. It beeps 10 times. You dig each time. 7 times you find a real coin. 3 times it's a bottle cap. Its **precision** is 7 out of 10. In plain words: when it beeps, how often is it right?

Precision only looks at the beeps. It says nothing about coins you walked past without a beep. That's what recall measures.

In the lesson's example, a "beep" is the model saying "yes," like flagging a payment as fraud. Two of the three counts matter here:

- `tp` (true positive): the model said yes, and it really was yes. A real coin.
- `fp` (false positive): the model said yes, but it was really no. A bottle cap.

Precision is then:

```
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
```

The bottom part, `tp + fp`, is every time the model said yes. The top part, `tp`, is the times it was right. So precision is the share of its "yes" answers you can trust.

High precision means few false alarms.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The model is too small for the task”?
check:0:0.a:
"The model is too small for the task" sounds reasonable, because small models can struggle. But it doesn't fit the numbers.

A model that's too small can't capture the patterns in the data. Think of it as having too little room to learn. If that were the problem, it would do badly everywhere, including on the test set. It would not score 97 in 100 in testing.

What we actually see is a big gap: great in testing, much worse in production. That gap is the clue. It says the test score was too optimistic, not that the model was too weak.

The question also tells us that rows from the same users appeared in both training and test. So the model may have memorised those users' habits. The test then quizzed it on people it already knew. Real users in production are new to it, so the score drops.

"Leakage: the test users were in training too" is better because it explains both the inflated test score and the drop in production, using the fact the question gives you.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The test set was too large to score fairly”?
check:0:2.a:
That option points at the wrong thing. A test set being large doesn't make a score unfair. If anything, more test rows give you a *more* trustworthy score, because one lucky or unlucky row matters less.

It does get one thing right: something about the test was off, since 97 dropped to 70. But size can't explain a score that's too *high*. A bigger exam doesn't make students look smarter than they are.

It also ignores the biggest clue in the question: rows from the same users were in both training and test. That means the model had already seen those users' habits during training. At test time, it partly recognised them instead of predicting fresh. That's like seeing exam questions in advance. The score looks great, then real users in production (the live system) show its true level.

"Leakage: the test users were in training too" is better because it explains both the inflated test score and the drop in production, using the exact clue the question gives you.

check:1:0.q: Why not “At random, ticket by ticket”?
check:1:0.a:
Picking at random, ticket by ticket, does get one thing right. It mixes the data well, so training and test look similar overall. For many problems, that's fine.

The trouble here is that each customer wrote many tickets. Split at random, and the same customer almost always lands on both sides. Their writing style, their product and their usual complaints all appear in training. The model can learn "this customer tends to say X" instead of what tickets mean in general. Then the test set asks about that same customer, and the model looks smarter than it is.

That's **leakage**: information about the test set sneaking into training. The test score comes out inflated. Later, in **production** (the live system real users depend on), new customers show up that the model has never seen, and the results disappoint.

Splitting by customer is better because it keeps all of a customer's tickets on one side, so the test measures how the model does on people it has truly never met.

check:1:2.q: Why not “By length, short ones go to test”?
check:1:2.a:
Splitting by length does one thing right. It is a clear rule, and each ticket lands on exactly one side. No single ticket gets counted twice.

But it misses the real danger. One customer usually writes both short and long tickets. So that customer's short tickets go to test while their long ones go to training. The model has already seen how that person writes, their product and their usual problems. When it meets their short tickets in test, it is partly recognising a familiar customer, not showing it learned something general. That is **leakage**, and it makes the test score look better than it really is.

There is a second problem. The test set would contain only short tickets. In production, the live system real users depend on, tickets come in every length. So the score would only tell you how the model handles short ones, not the mix it will actually face.

Splitting by customer is better because every ticket from a customer stays on one side, so the test truly measures how the model does on people it has never seen.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Whether the model is big enough”?
check:2:1.a:
Model size is a fair thing to wonder about in general. It's one of the choices you make when building a model. But it doesn't fit this situation.

The clue in the question is that 99% "feels too good to be true." That's a worry about the score itself: can you trust it? Checking the model's size tells you nothing about that. A score is only meaningful if the test set holds data the model has never seen. If that isn't true, the number is inflated however the model was built.

So the first thing to question is the test, not the model. If the same document sits in both training and test, the model may simply be recognising something it already studied, not sorting a new document. That's **leakage**: information from the test set slipping into training. The lesson calls it the most common reason a model that looked great disappoints in production, meaning the live system real users depend on.

"Whether a document is in both sets" is better because it directly checks whether the 99% is honest, which is exactly what the suspicious score is warning you about.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Whether the test set has enough rows”?
check:2:2.a:
It's a fair thought, just not the first thing to check.

**What it gets right:** a tiny test set can mislead. If there are only 20 documents, getting them all right could be luck. So size does matter for how much you trust a score.

**What it misses:** a bigger test set doesn't fix the usual cause of "too good to be true." If the same documents sit in both training and test, the model has already seen the answers. It can score 99% on 10 rows or 10,000 rows. Adding more rows just gives you a bigger, equally inflated score.

That's leakage: information from the test set slipping into training. The lesson calls it the most common reason a model looks great in testing and then disappoints in production, the live system real users depend on.

**Why "Whether a document is in both sets" is better:** it checks directly for leakage, the likeliest explanation for a suspiciously high score, so it tells you whether the 99% means anything at all.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Don't test on what you trained on” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
A test is only useful if it checks something the model hasn't already seen. If an example sits in both your training data and your test data, the model can just remember the answer. The score looks great, but it tells you nothing about new cases. This is called **leakage**: information from the test set "leaks" into training.

**A small example.** You build a churn model, which predicts which customers will cancel. Customer `u7` has 50 rows of activity. You shuffle all rows and split them randomly. Now 40 of `u7`'s rows land in training and 10 in test. The model learns `u7`'s habits, then "predicts" those 10 test rows easily. You report 95% accuracy.

**What happens in real work.** You ship it. Real customers it has never met show up, and accuracy drops to 70%. The team trusted the 95% and made plans around it. Now they have to explain the gap.

**The fix:**
- Remove duplicate rows first, so the same example can't appear twice.
- Split by user or document, not by row. Then every row for one user goes to the same side, either all in training or all in test.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
The main warning sign is **a score that looks too good**. Watch for these:

- **Test score almost matches training score.** A model usually does a bit worse on data it hasn't seen. If the two are nearly identical and both very high, be suspicious.
- **A big drop after launch.** It scored great in testing, then disappoints in production (the live system real users depend on). This is the classic sign of leakage.
- **Strong on familiar users, weak on new ones.** If new customers get much worse predictions than existing ones, the model may have memorised people rather than learned patterns.
- **Missing or vague records.** In MLflow, open the run. If there's no `split` parameter, or it doesn't say `by_user`, nobody can prove the split was honest.

**Quickest check:** list every user in the training data and every user in the test data, then look for names that appear in both. That shared group is called the overlap. It should be empty. Even one shared user means the test score is inflated. Fix the split, retrain, and expect a lower, but honest, number.

learn:stops.a:
The rule "keep each user on one side" is a good start, but some situations need more care.

**When data changes over time**, splitting by user is not enough, because patterns from the future can leak into training. Train on older dates and test on the newest ones, so the test looks like tomorrow's real traffic.

**With an LLM or RAG app** (a chatbot that looks up your documents before answering), you often aren't training a model at all, but leakage still happens. If your test questions show up in prompt examples or in the documents it searches, the score is inflated, so keep a test set you never use while tuning prompts.

**With very little data**, one test set may hold too few users to trust its score. Use cross-validation instead: split the users into several groups, let each group take a turn as the test set, and average the scores.

learn:term.a:
Think of a student who memorises last year's exam answers. They score perfectly on that exact paper. Give them new questions on the same topic and they struggle. They learned the answers, not the skill.

That is **overfitting**. The model gets so good at its training data that it remembers the exact rows, quirks and all, instead of the general pattern behind them.

You spot it by watching two scores while the model trains. The training score keeps rising. The validation score, from data held back for tuning, stops improving and then drops. That widening gap is the sign the model is memorising rather than learning.

In the lesson's example, this is why every row from `u1` and `u7` goes only to `test`. If some of their rows were also in `train`, the model could memorise those users. The test score would look great, but it would be measuring memory, not skill. Keeping those users out of training means the test honestly asks: does this work on people the model has never seen?

judge.notes: Passes all checks. The last paragraph describes leakage without naming it, which is a minor weakness: naming leakage would keep it distinct from overfitting.

check:0:1.a:
"A timeout" doesn't fit what happened. A timeout is about no answer coming back. Here an answer did come back. The assistant quoted "Policy HR-114, section 3" as if it were real.

So the problem isn't a missing reply. The problem is what the reply says. It points to a source that doesn't exist.

The lesson lists this exact case under hallucination: "A fake source: it quotes a policy page that doesn't exist." It happens because the model writes what is likely, not what is checked. A policy number with a section sounds likely, so the model writes one, in a sure tone.

What "A timeout" gets right: something did go wrong. What it misses is the kind of wrong. Calling it a timeout would send you to fix the wrong thing. The lesson's fixes target hallucination instead. Give the model the real documents (RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation: answering from your documents, not from memory). Tell it to say so when the policy is silent. Add cases like this to your eval set.

"A hallucination" is better because it names the real problem: a confident answer that isn't true, here a made-up policy.

check:0:2.a:
"A rate limit" is a real thing that can go wrong when you use an AI service. So it's a fair guess. But it doesn't fit what happened here.

A **rate limit** is a cap on how many requests you can send in a set time, like "60 per minute." Go over it, and the service refuses. You get an error, often "429 Too Many Requests." In other words, you get *no answer*.

In this question, the assistant *did* answer. It quoted "Policy HR-114, section 3" in a sure tone. The trouble is that the policy doesn't exist. A rate limit can't produce that. It blocks answers. It doesn't invent them.

What happened is the model wrote what *sounded* likely. HR answers often cite a policy number, so it made one up. Nothing checked it against real documents. That's the "fake source" pattern from the lesson.

"A hallucination" is better because it names exactly this: a confident answer, here a made-up source, that isn't true.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the warning signs that hallucination, randomness or unfairness slipped past you.

**A score that looks too good.** Your eval (a set of questions with known right answers) passes at 100%, then users report wrong answers. Often the eval was run once, or only on easy questions.

**Answers with no source behind them.** In your traces (the step-by-step record of what the agent did), the answer quotes a policy or a number, but no retrieved document contains it. That is a likely hallucination.

**Never saying "I don't know".** Logs show zero "not covered, ask HR" replies, even for odd questions. A healthy system admits gaps sometimes.

**Same question, different results.** A test passes on Monday and fails on Tuesday with no change. The model's randomness was never measured.

**Name-swapped pairs disagree.** "Ana" and "Ahmed" ask the same leave question and get different answers.

**Quickest check:** pick ten real answers. Look for each key claim in the retrieved source. Run each question three times. Swap one name. Any claim with no source, any flip, or any name gap means a step was skipped.

judge.notes: No major problem. The closing line 'means a step was skipped' slightly overstates, since an unsupported claim is only a likely hallucination.

learn:stops.a:
The rule "keep each claim the source doesn't back" works well for short, exact claims. Here is where it needs extra care.

**The answer says it in different words.** "Five leftover days roll over" means the same as "5 unused days carry over", but an exact text match calls it unsupported. In real apps, compare meaning instead, often by asking a second LLM to judge whether the source backs each claim.

**The source itself is out of date.** If the policy changed last month but your documents didn't, a claim can match the source and still be wrong. Keep your documents current, and store the date of each source so you can spot stale ones.

**There are thousands of documents.** Checking every claim against every page gets slow and noisy. Check each claim only against the few passages your RAG step retrieved, meaning the chunks it pulled in to answer that question.

learn:term.a:
A **hallucination** is when an AI gives an answer that sounds sure but isn't true.

**An everyday comparison:** picture a new coworker who hates saying "I don't know." You ask about the leave policy. They haven't read it, so they give you a number that *sounds* right, in a calm, confident voice. They aren't lying on purpose. They're guessing what a policy usually says.

An LLM (large language model, the kind of AI behind chat tools) works a bit like that. It writes what is *likely* to come next, not what it has *checked*. So it can state a made-up rule or quote a page that doesn't exist, with no hint of doubt.

**In the lesson's example:**

```python
source = ["5 unused days carry over"]
answer = ["30 unused days carry over"]
```

The `source` is the real policy. The `answer` is what the AI said. "30 unused days" sounds plausible, but the source never says it. That claim is **unsupported**: nothing backs it up. That makes it a likely hallucination.

It's like checking a report against the receipts. Any amount without a receipt gets questioned.
